The Bluewing searobin (Prionotus punctatus) exhibits early life-history traits that are tightly coupled to water temperature. During yolk-sac resorption, the lecithotrophic larvae remain dependent on endogenous reserves until the onset of exogenous feeding. Field observations indicate that at a stable incubation temperature of 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C], the period from fertilization to hatching lasts approximately 7.7 days [ab = approximately 7.7 days]. Newly emerged prolarvae possess a minute yolk-sac, and their wet weight at birth is estimated to be 0.00061 grams [Wwb = 0.00061 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of the closely related northern searobin, Prionotus carolinus. This extremely small initial mass reflects the pelagic egg strategy common among triglid fishes, wherein a large number of small, buoyant eggs are spawned into the water column. The rapid depletion of yolk reserves under these thermal conditions forces the larva to quickly develop feeding structures to avoid the point of no return.

As the pelagic larval phase progresses, the planktonic exogenously feeding larva undergoes significant allometric growth. The transition from a preflexion to a postflexion larva is marked by the ossification of fin rays and the onset of scale formation. Published growth curves for the species, based on otolith microchemistry from wild-caught individuals, suggest that under the prevailing thermal regime of 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C], the maximum lifespan may extend to approximately 19 years [am = approximately 19 years]. This longevity is notable among searobins, which are generally considered relatively short-lived demersal fishes. The attainment of such an advanced age is likely facilitated by the species' benthic, reef-associated habitat, which provides refuge from pelagic predators. Comparative data from congeners indicate that metabolic rates scale predictably with body mass, supporting the gradual accumulation of somatic tissue over decades.

Sexual maturation in the Bluewing searobin involves a pronounced increase in body size before the onset of gonadal recrudescence. Individuals reach the total length at puberty when they measure 26.2 centimeters [Lp = 26.2 centimeters], a milestone that corresponds to the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. At this length, the calculated wet weight at puberty is 168 grams [Wwp = 168 grams], based on a length-weight conversion factor of 0.00933. The relationship between length and mass in this species appears to be strongly isometric, meaning that condition factor remains relatively constant throughout the sub-adult stage. This consistency suggests that juveniles allocate resources efficiently toward both somatic growth and energy storage. The onset of vitellogenesis in females is tightly synchronized with seasonal temperature cycles, ensuring that the energetically expensive process of egg production coincides with periods of high prey availability.

Reproductive output in Prionotus punctatus is characterized by a high fecundity that compensates for the high mortality rates experienced during the pelagic larval stage. Under controlled conditions at 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C], adult females produce approximately 493 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 493 eggs per day], which can be sustained over an extended spawning season. This daily egg production rate represents a maximum reproductive output that is comparable to that of the striped searobin, Prionotus evolans, a closely related species with a similar life-history strategy. The ultimate female wet weight recorded for the Bluewing searobin is 850 grams [Wwi = 850 grams], a value that is achieved when individuals reach their asymptotic total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters]. Large, gravid females contribute disproportionately to the annual egg complement due to their greater body cavity volume and higher metabolic capacity.

The demography of the Bluewing searobin is shaped by its life-history trade-offs between early fecundity and somatic maintenance. A gravid individual at the onset of its first spawning event carries a substantial investment in oocytes, having already attained a body mass of 168 grams [Wwp = 168 grams] at the total length of 26.2 centimeters [Lp = 26.2 centimeters]. The transition from a reproductively immature sub-adult to a breeding adult involves a nearly fivefold increase in wet weight to reach the ultimate female mass of 850 grams [Wwi = 850 grams]. This significant investment in growth before reproduction suggests an iteroparous strategy where adult survival is prioritized over early reproductive output. Field surveys indicate that senescent individuals, which have completed their reproductive lifespan, eventually succumb to natural mortality after approximately 19 years [am = approximately 19 years] in the wild, a duration consistent with the slow pace of life characteristic of larger-bodied triglids at a temperature of 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C].
